title: 'The Music of Hoagy Carmichael' with Bob Wilber
summary: Bob Wilber and producer Bill Borden heard her at the Riverboat and used her on a Monmouth-Evergreen Carmichael album with members of the World's Greatest Jazz Band.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

Very good.
All right, we're just coming back from a pause. And we're going to turn now to an album that doesn't a recording date on the line notes.
I saw a reference somewhere to it as being in 1968. But Maxine just told me that she thought it was recorded in January or February of '69.

Well it had to be in January or February of '69, because I had gone into the Riverboat with Bobby Hackett January 3, 1969.
And it was during that time that Bob came in Wilber and mentioned the fact that he was going to do this Hoagy Carmichael album.
And he had spoken to Bill Borden, a producer, suggesting that they have a vocal on the album; because it doesn't make sense to have a Hoagy Carmichael and not have any vocal.
So, Bill Borden was interested in like

In fact, Borden, at one time, was the -- did some arranging with Claude Thornhill when he had his band.
And so Bob mentioned the fact that I was at the Riverboat. And I think somewhere along the line, I might've done a gig with Bob Wilber some place -- a private affair -- and he had heard me.
So, he suggested Maxine Sullivan. So Bill Borden hadn't really heard -- he might've heard me years ago.
He came down to the Riverboat and he heard me sing, and he agreed that we should do it.
So this had to be around February or January of '39. Because it couldn't have been '38 --

That was somewhat of a beginning of something or other.
Naturally by being the music of Hoagy Carmichael, I was confined to those selections that were written by Hoagy Carmichael. You know, "Georgia On My Mind", "Skylark" --
A lovely song.
Yeah. I loved them all. "In The Cool, Cool, Cool of the Evening", "Rocking Chair", and "I Get Along Without You".

And 'I Get Along Without You Very Well.' I had known these songs for quite some time, and I like to do them. But I was very pleased when Bill Borden said, 'Well, you know you can record these....' more or less' -- apologizing for the fact that I was limited to these Hoagy Carmichael tunes. So he said -- and, of course, the arrangements, too. They were pretty big arrangements. And I think I mintioned to him that I preferred to work with a small group. So he said after we made this album, that I could make another one and I could do songs of my own choosing, and use a smaller group.
This is essentially a version of The World's Greatest Jazz Band, isn't it?
Yes, it is. Most of the guys on here were with The World's Greatest Jazz Band, except Bernie Privin, of course, and Bernie Layton. Bob Wilber, you know -- it was his date.

He had Bud Freeman who was with The World's Greatest Jazz Band, Yank Lawson and --
One of the co-leaders?
Yeah, one of the co-leaders of The World's Greatest Jazz Band.
And I noticed that they had George Duvivier on bass instead of Bob Haggart. He may have been out of town, or something.
But most of these guys were with The World's Greatest Jazz Band, you know, that I joined after I finished an engagement with Bobby Hackett.
Yeah.
